chunks: SoC versus separate components. The question: What are some tradeoffs between going for a SoC vs all separate components?
You can build a product's electronics as one integrated chip (a SoC, "What is a system on chip") or as several separate chips on a board.
One chip is smaller, uses less energy to move data, and is cheaper per unit when you make many. The price is a big one-time design cost and less freedom to change parts later.
So the right choice depends mostly on how many units you will make.
Think of moving boxes inside one house versus between buildings across town. Inside the house, you carry a box a few steps.
Across town, you load a truck, drive, and unload, which takes more time and fuel. A SoC is the house: data moves short distances. Separate chips are the buildings.
The picture misses one thing: designing a custom house costs a lot up front, while renting existing buildings costs almost nothing to start.
Below about 180,000 units the discrete board has the lower average cost because the SoC's NRE is spread over too few chips.
Above it the SoC wins and approaches its 18 USD floor, while the discrete design flattens near 45 USD.
Change the NRE or unit costs and the crossover moves, which is the real content of the answer.
Energy per bit: the energy needed to send one 0 or 1 across a link. Shorter wires cost less.
NRE (non-recurring engineering): the one-time cost of designing, verifying and making the chip. Unit cost: what it costs to make each extra chip once the design exists.
Break-even volume: the number of units where two options cost the same in total. Respin: a new version of the chip made to fix a bug, which costs time and money.
Compare a custom SoC with a board of separate chips. The SoC has an NRE of 5,000,000 USD and costs 18 USD per unit. The board has an NRE of 150,000 USD and costs 45 USD per unit.
The SoC saves 27 USD per unit but costs 4,850,000 USD more up front. Break-even is 4 850 000 over 27 about 180 000 units. Below that, the board is cheaper. Above it, the SoC wins.
That is the whole idea.
"Integration wins on size, power, speed and unit cost at volume: on-die wires are shorter and cheaper to drive than package pins and traces, and you cut packages, passives and board area.
It loses on upfront NRE, schedule, flexibility and process compromises, and heat is concentrated.
So integrate when volume and size or power limits justify the NRE, and use discrete parts or a module for low volume or uncertain requirements."
